fileDesc.titleStmt: MARTHA LADY GIFFARD HER LIFE AND CORRESPONDENCE (1664-1722). A SEQUEL TO THE LETTERS OF DOROTHY OSBORNE. ED. BY JULIA G. LUNGE. LONDON: GEORGE ALLEN & SONS. 1911.

text.p: For my Lady Berkeley, at Sir John Temple's House, at East Sheen, near Mortlake.
July 29.

I did not expect to hear ire Father was in Town, but am mighty glad you have him with you to help to put ire business in order before you leave it. I am vexed to have forgot in my last to desire the Bill of Betty's plate,
which would be the same to me to have payed for before you came away, pray send the bill as soon as you have it, & tell me where the money shall be left. If you bring the plate down with you will be time enouf for I hope we shall see you before her birtheday & till then all but the comb box it to be a profound secret. My correspondence with my niece begins now to mend I write to her & she only makes use of Mell Valerie to doe it to me. By the account of what keeps her in London I still conclude we shall not see her soon, and by your Brothers not coming before you yt your Father does not like ire company well enouff to come along with you.

I am very well content that business should be ordered as you may all be best pleased with it, & since I cannot fetch you heither perhaps you may carry me back with you when you go. Pray tell ire Father I have so many sorts of tea for him to taste that I doubt he will not stay long enough to try one every day. One came just now from Mr. Henley which I have not yet tasted but sure it must be something extraordinary for I never asked for any nor ever heard him talk of it. I will keep his letter till I see you which is full of the good humour of having so well succeeded in his Election. Mr. Norton's doom will not be passed till Monday. I wrote ire Father so long a letter last post I dare not answer one I received from him today till ire next, when ire sister's Bill for her money shall go with it. Thank God Papa is not very bad, I hear him just now going down stairs though with a lame knee. I will not brag of our melons till you come to taste them though I fancy nobody has succeeded better this year. Mr. Montague is successful in all things. I heard one say t'other day he had so much power in ye House he could persuade them to vote a man a horse if he had a mind to it. If Mr. Danvers be out I doubt he has showed some of it there but I hear he went to the office as he said he would doe last Monday. Adieu ire next I hope will tell us when we are to see you.
For my Lady Berkeley at Sir John Temple's House, near Mortlake, East Sheen.

You will wonder less when you find how glad I was to be rid of you that you have never heard from me since our worthy Postman never called for ye letters a Friday and his excuse today is his horse was up to ye Belly in a Bog but I believe he was up to the throat with a bottle which he has promised shall never be again and you must be content by it for once to have two letters to East Sheen together, and to tell you how my time has past since you went I have had less pain as well as less entertainment, once I ventured abroad last week when I found there nobody to chide me and was mch the better for it, but today I could not help wishing you could have bin at Mooreparke with four steps so you could have walked with me as I did first to another puddle in the gravvel walk and then out of it. Papa wishes you hear to, at a piece of roast beef at dinner which he eat for the first time with a very good stomach and I must tell you is now a great deal better, whatever comes after it. He has bin mighty weary with his hand since you went but all the old pains begin now to wear off, and he complains yet of no new ones. I will not ask how you liked ye House yt dismal day next time I hope you will choose a better and tell me.

I did not intend you should have thought of anything I desired besides writing to me till you had less to think of for ire self. But one thing I think is absolutely necessary yt I once spoke to you of when I was here, yt I should some day or other send a compliment to my Lady Essex when she is in Town.

If ever you have occasion to send Mrs. Kilby to London
I desire she may doe it for me, and yt you will take some of the fault on yourself that it came no sooner. I leave the compliment to you to make for me and desire to know what reception your mantel had. I have not heard from Wickham since you went but had a letter from Petworth yesterday with Herrings which we all wished you some of. Lady Scarborough was there still but to go home to-day. Ye Duke of Somerset returns this week but I fancy neither will happen without a better fit of weather then it is likely should come this year. Tell ire Father I will find some way of sending him Virgil as soon as I have read it my self. We are well advanced in Ogelbie since you went and you will be too happy when you are here too, to have read Homer before it, but you will want Doll to put you in mind as she does us of everything we have forgot. Papa and I desire my Lt Berkeley should know yt we approve of all things of his taking Lt Ovary's House. I hope his Lady received a letter I wrote her since you went in answer to hers which I wish you could tell me without asking her for I have had sad luck since I saw you, with some letters which I hope will never befall me with yours. Adieu.
For my Lady Berkeley, at her house in Dover Street, London.

You certainly staid at Moor Park as long as it has to be endured and I am mightily comforted to have lost you since I rose this morning and saw all ye ground covered with snow which. never happened before in October as many years as my life has lasted and was but in May yt I was ready to cry to see all my cammellias discovered in it. You will be glad to hear in ye midst of it that Papa is so well as to have dined below every day since you went so yt I have not wanted something to revive me, while the weather was good I endeavoured to do it with walking as long in the gravel walk as you fancied me the day you left us the Horses came no more where they went out if the coachman is to be found who I suppose you helped to come home better. I had a letter from the Duchesses of Somerset who is very sorry (to tell you her own words) she shall not have the happiness to see La Berkeley at Petworth this year, which she had so long pleased herself with she says she has drunk as good a tea at Almay as she had tasted these seven years so I have desired ire sister today to buy half a pound and divide it between ire Father and I if we both like it I will send for some more, but pray let me have your opinion too and another request I have yt you pay for it viz. 3 guineas a pound I am sorry you were not hear to read my Lord Sunderland's letter you knew before yt he was to be hear next May but you did not
know that I was to go back with him and yt against yt time Mr. Henley is to be desired to take his measures better. I had a letter from ire cousin Temple today telling me her affairs is so well advanced yt she hopes to se us again soon, and have heard more since then I wish of the effects of her remedy though I would not have it go further, yet Mary's servants say they have taken his vomits till they were hardly able to drag their legs after them and indeed Mary does look as if she would never recover it but the worst is I find the children have taken them too. I should not have told you this but I feared you or any of ire friends might be drawn in as I was almost one day yt my stomach was very ill and I certainly had eaten a pear yt was offered me but yt I happened to ask if it would not make me vomit which you know is never my inclinations, she said not unless it met with some humours which I could not answer it shd not doe, with many ill ones in me. All this I must out with when she comes and try to keep the children out of his hands I wish I may come off well at this rate if I go on you will know as much of Moore Park as if you sat still in your little corner by my fireside. I wish I may find no more to tell you. I had a letter from L. Berkeley today but mentions nothing of what I write about. Ye reasons for not venturing in this weather yt I will never believe he takes ill or yt anybody can think so desolate as we are here yt such friends would not be welcome. I think ye Duchess of Grafton since she has been able to govern her life no better is very discreet to let somebody else doe it for her. Ire maid shall be remembered and sent with a bundle of all the other things we agreed upon, pray don't spare ye cheese I can furnish you with another when yt is gon but believe you have letter enough to serve you for a great while. I had a very good one from Jack to-day and hope soon to hear yt ire other Brother has arrived I writ to your Father a Friday. Adieu.
For My Lady Berkeley, at her House in Dover Street, London.
November 28, 1697/8.

I am sorry my ugly Velvet gives you so much trouble. I will not send this back unless you tell me you have got one much thinner for I am satisfied to have bin out myself in thinking it much to dear, those I mentioned being a great deal warmer, if you light on one of the wearthe of this yt you think much thinner send it me on Wednesday and this shall be returned next day, else I shall be very well content to make use of it having not only bin very cold at Church to-day but ever since I came home. I think it was being struck with hearing poor Mr. Kelsey prayed for just at ye point of death who was at Church last Sunday and I doubt got ye illness there which carried him away. You know ire uncle and he had always compared notes about ye gout ever since he came heither, but yt he has lately bin better off and dyed now of a fever if he be dead as we expected when I came home and is the greatest loss we could have here out of our family, being a very good doctor and a better friend, and has left nobody behind him I should care to send to in any extreme it is well I think this letter should end which must all be melancholy and yt I find by yours I received just now you need not anything to increase. I would fine for yt reason have you go abroad, though for my own part yt am in a desert I doe not think I should find less to trouble me in any other sort of life or company and if you could compose ire self as not to let ye remembrance of what is past disturb wht you have left I fancy ire life would not be very uneasy. I am sure you have too much sense not to think this reasonable and the thoughts that make ire dreams so you must try to change them if you would be rid of the
others. I would fine advise about ire reading what I practise myself not to read anything very serious before you go to bed; that would be a good time to read Virgil in, and let ire Turkish history only go on a days. You don't tell me nor anybody else whether my Lt Berkeley comes or no, if he does I will be more sure to doe as you desire and for ire maid I will tell you perfectly how ye case stands, I never saw a greater diligence then Nannie, what I wrote about nor is it possible for anybody to have a better servant yet yt has not at all changed my thoughts of parting with her and I fancy too would be glad to have a mistress, yt did not keep a better sort of servant to such a one I could recommend her. I hope you will help as ire Cousin Temple has promised to enquire for her till she is provided so I cannot resolve now and have promised to see one here but both those you mention I fancy more fit to be such a servant as I believe Nanny would be where one keeps never a better. You know all I can say now but not parting with her soon we must not hinder them from providing themselves.
Papa continues pretty well I hope to tell you I am better next post in the meantime desire you will excuse me to your Cousin Temple yt I doe not thank her for her letter by this. Adieu.

note.value: MARTHA TEMPLE TO JANE MARTHA TEMPLE

text.p:
I must begin by giving you thanks for my tippet than which. a better present and a more useful one to me was never chosen, and I hope to be in a little better credit both with my Lady Berkeley and you that the first service Lattice did for me was to take of the black tassells and put on gold ones. I am sorry to say I doubt it will be ye last, but such a mistake between you and I never happened nor I fancy never will again, it's my wish to tell you all that has happened in this little time, but the minuet I saw her I concluded my service and she and I were never made for one another, I am ready to chide
you for thinking I was, were we ill bred or so ill-mannered as to employ her in such things as I have noebody else to doe for me. She deserves the little I know of her the best service in England, and desires that she go lest he fall in love with her, she owns never to have washed a room in her life, and when she rose next morning asked if she must make her own bed, complained yt she should not be able to wait and work in a room without a fire and you know I have no other, but the cruel thing of all was dining with common servants and yt she said she had never reckoned upon and doubted she should not be able to bear, indeed I believe nobody had a greater right yet when I spoke to her today how sorry I was to have put her upon what I doubted she yt had lived in much better places must think very hard and she could not be more uneasy than I should be every time I did it, but was such a servant I wanted, she said she had rather enter upon any service than live any longer out of it, and in yt I believe told the on reason but she has lived I find in great places, and bin an absolute gentlewoman and I dare say is one by her name and her friends, for I have had a great deal of talk with her, her journey shall be paid for and Mrs Bradly that came down with her will go up with her again a Monday, Nanny Logger who I had ordered to go yt day says she is very happy to stay longer and so I am going in search of puzzle again, 3 gentlewomen had bin a little too much state as I make use of my cousin Dingley whenever I am in want. Hetty's place being the height of her ambition.

To talk of something else what you write me in ire. last abt. the quarrel between Lt L and Mr. M. was the first words I had heard of it. I must beg of you never to avoid writing to me anything you can spare time for upon ye fancy yt I hear it from others for though it happen as it seldom does be told from all hands, such different circumstances which all of them help to make me understand is better, and is pleasanter very often than the thing
itself, the reply in that though was very extraordinary and one sees by it how people help towards making themselves so many enemies. I had an answer today of the question I told you I asked in my last about the secretary's money. He says he has amounts for 2500 but by accounts of other years signed by his brother's hand he thinks he has pretence for several sums for journeys and other things which when he knows more exactly he will tell me. I have sent him with another compliment from Papa to ye King where I fancy he is not displeased with finding occasions of going.

You give me an account today which much enlightens me on all that has happened I must make yt letter ye compliment of saying yt I find noebody better informed. I do not know from whence yt comes but I desire to be acquainted with some of those yt you say are so kind to see you still, who will be as much in my favour as you are in there's, more when Christmas is over you may see any yt you would have entertained at other times in a nightgoune and then ye great scarf will serve. I am glad Lt Berkeley writes too us who I have wrote part of Lattice's story to, she vows you will tell her and I flatter myself both of you be of my mind yt have to make anybody miserable or indeed when I can help it, to be which I am sure she would have bin every day.
I am sorry my paper is done though I am still to write to ye Duchess of Somerset. Adieu.

note.value: LADY GIFFARD'S LETTER TO LADY BERKELEY.
MARTHA TEMPLE TO JANE MARTHA TEMPLE

text.p: For my Lady Berkeley, Dover Street, London. Petworth, Sept. 7, 14, 1698.

We are got hither at last, and Papa I thank God very well, and so insufferably pert with winning 12 guineas at Crimp last night. The Duke of Somerset says he never remembers seeing him better. We came a Monday in the evening and just before the Duchess had a letter from La. Scarborough to tell her she went to London today for a fortnight, and intended to se me at Moore Park as she went by, so your charm is not yet ended wh. hindered us from meeting two summers, but I had a letter yesterday from her to desire that it may be when the Duchess of Somerset comes to stay there a fortnight, wh. is to be as soon as she returns from London and while the Duke goes to Marlborough. When she is there pray enquire a great deal of our East India ships with wh. she is concerned as well as I, and nobody can inform you better of what I most desire to know is whether I may take part of my share in what I like or must be obliged to have it all in money if tic divided which whether it be much or little to me would make a great difference. And now I must tell you what misfortunes have, I hear befalled some of your friends and mine. My Lt. Portland and Monsr. Overkerke I hear have had a quarrel at Loo, and the last they say treated him like a dog which I am apt enough to believe, for people are too apt to insult when one is falling and when nobody will help to right one. I believe one has seldom the heart to do anything towards it themselves, this they say has extremely exalted another person, and altogether tic thought more than my Lt. Portland can bear altogether any longer, that he may not want a companion in his
afternoons, I hear that Mrs. Howard came t'other day from where Mrs. Billingsly had order to take ye care the children from her and when she came to my Lord of Essex' lodgings at London, she found a padlock. Upon that she could not get in which Mr. Billingsly said he had my Lord Essex's order for. You know whether I am rightly informed in all this, and pray send a yd of muslin for pinners and ten yards of crowsfoot to edge it with to Mrs. Hanbury before you leave town, the Dke. and Dchess. of Richmond dine here to-day and so my news and my letter are at an end together.
Adieu I desire you will send word to East Sheen what is become of it, there is now no doubt of our being home to receive our letters on Friday.
You never told me what became of ?

note.value: LETTER I: LADY GIFFARD'S LETTERS TO LADY PORTLAND.
MARTHA TEMPLE TO JANE MARTHA TEMPLE

text.p: To the Countess of Portland at the Hague. July 14, 1700.

You have made the best amends you can for the want I find of your company here by this and others kind letters received from you last week which will always contribute as much as anything can do towards making me happy and easy. I have not been alone here for a whole week since I came and yet you not be in pain whenever it happens to me again, I will assure you it passed much better in this place itself than I expected and made me reflect often upon what I learnt early in my life that custom will make everything easy. I am not likely I believe to make the trial any more till towards winter. Lt. Berkeley came down last Wednesday and ire. Mother and sister have soon promised me a visit you know our life if you remember how it used to pass last summer, only yt. I am always alone when they are not with me which did not use to happen then, but since you tell me you are so well I will complain of nothing while I have hopes of seeing you again so soon as my Lt. Portland promised but if you should serve me so basely (as they would make me believe) and not come next winter is what I am not at all prepared for, and therefore am inclined not to think it is so much believed here yt I was asked what the Deputy Statholders place is worth to my Lord Portland that it obliged him to leave England, I have asked him myself last Post what I am to believe of it and therefore will leave it for another thing I am to know of you, if there be any trouble in yt I was told yt before my Lord Portland left Windsor he sent to ye Princess to know how many Bucks he shd have orders to kill for her use this year and yt she was angry to be asked and said she would order as many
as she had a mind too herself, this put me in mind of what you told me of your taking leave there and my Lt of the Prince and made me resolve to write you what I heard of it. I did long to have a letter from you after the King was landed and now I am writing this it is come and mighty glad I am of the news it brings me of His Majesty's Health which I hope ye air of Loo will quite recover him for I assure you he was not at all well when he went over. You know I would have all my friends make their court there and therefore am very well pleased with what you tell me of one of them but most of all with the hopes you give me of seeing you att Windsor Park before winter. I find my Lord Berkeley thinks of staying but till Michaelmas and being so well at London I have a great deal of reason to take it kindly they should do it so long, I intend not to move till you fetch me away and if yt is not to be all the winter you don't know what you may have to answer for.

Ye Duchess of Somerset and ye Duke is going to Zion for a fortnight yt my Lt Northumberland may breathe the air of ye country which ye Doctors have advised. I had no time her being ill writ for my company both intended must be delayed for some time but we think to go to ye Grange some day this week and then you shall have an account of both Master and Mistress of whom I have heard nothing lately but kindly condole with my Lt. Portland for the loss of his friend my Lt. Privy Seal who by the character I have heard of him think it ye greatest loss could happen to ye King and ye Nation. I find you have ye account of my disappointment from Honing which I must own to what I never expected could happen to me but with luck and misfortune, risk it - as would quite have made me insensible to it which I will not pretend to so much philosophy as to say I am now but to bear it and everything as well as I can; shall be ye endeavour of my whole life. I give you and another friend a great many thanks for your offer and concern,
but nothing can be done till ye King comes over and before yt I hope you will both be here to advise me.

Did you hear Lord Hertford advised ye King to cut of general pensions, and that just before his journey my Lt. Steven was struck out, and all his relations. I shall envy you the journey to Rotterdam upon ye East India ships coming in if you carry ye pocket full of money but I try to think ye greatest fortune yt could befall anybody but I believe it is all to be disposed of in commission and I fancy you have quite spoiled ye design of getting ire money for ye first by offering to pay for this note. I have a great mind to chide you for I am mighty entertained with all you tell me from Holland which will make me troublesome with enquiring after some things I have quite forgot, one is who this Princess of Join is, her husband and mother-in-law, I knew very well, but must own to remember nothing of Mm. Hibrandst? I fancy by what she said to you she has as much forget me. It is melancholy to think of in the 22 years there should hardly be any body besides Mm. Portrocks who you say never very left of all so many as I knew att ye Hague. I believe you find the visits differ in many things from England where the men seldom appear and as I remember we are sure to see them oftener then the women. This puts me in remind of my Visitor my Lord Sunderland and who has bin very ill with the gout first in his toe and then in his stomach, they now fancy ye cholick but another of ye dear friends of mine is well and more easy than ever she was in her life, is to spend part of her summer as she says herself with ye Bishop of Salisbury and ye best is L. E. denys ever to have said anything to Mrs. B. yt was to ye disadvantage of Lt. P. she is to dine tomorrow with a friend of yours in St. James Place where she has invited herself, and be assured yt perhaps I may tell you more off her if you do not spoil my intelligence by taking notice of this.

Ire Brother Jack left us last Friday and I am soon
promised a visit from ire mother and sister Lucy. L. and La. Anglesea have both come into ye country and if as we ought to do I may believe in truth his Ldsp. is ye worst husband in the world, I have asked friends of't though they are not of that mind think it only his fondness and jealousy together yt makes him so ill to her which you know is not ye reason was given us of it. I know I shall not often have her to invite and therefore have as you remember of my time. Lt. and La. B. now look forward to their being here I may send a Billet in one of their paquets to my Lt. Portland to give him thanks for ye kind one I received in yrs as good friends as you reckon upon here the first thing he said coming from Church today was how happy we all were yt you were not with us. We had a Parson who was as bad as reading Homer. Lt. Berkeley sat in the corner where nobody saw him and was as bad as he used to be in my chamber and ire sister did nothing but jog me to look upon him and if you had bin there we had certainly all shamed ourselves, I doubt I have done it already with this long letter wh. has hardly left me room to bid dear La. Portland Adieu.
For the Countess of Portland at ye Hague. Dover St., July 18, 1707.
I wish I knew whether you care to hear from me, I am very sure I never sat down more unwillingly to write to you, or anybody who knew so little where to begin.

I am sure you know the share I have always had in all ire sufferings and my own in this will enough express
how surely I morn with you. I fancy my niece L. has told you all you care to know and I should be wrong to repeat anything yt could only serve to renew ire trouble. I know ire thoughts and mine have agreed so well upon all the cruel accidents of this kind we have gone through that you will endeavour to turn them as I am trying to do wholly to the care of the desolate family yt is left and such is ye kindest way of remembering what we have lost.

My Lt. Berkeley is now with me, and I am going to them tonight with my Nephew and niece to leave him my house very sorry that I cannot be in it with him but he seems to like it much better than anything else yt was proposed to him till he can return to his own. Yt I was glad it came into my head to make him ye offer.

I have bin little from him since I came to town and he seems never better pleased than in seeing any of her friends. He wishes often for you as ye greatest support and comfort he has to reckon upon, so I am sure you will ever be to him and indeed nobody ever wanted it more. He desired me to present his service to you but says it is impossible for him to write. I need say nothing to express how much he feels his loss to you, the thought of yt if anything could, would make us forget our own, but he is truth, extreme reasonable and disposed entirely to what I have begged of him, to turn his thoughts to ye business and care of his family, and while you are away to find he has a little help and yt I am fast growing so useless a creature yt should think nothing too much yt is in my power to serve him the difficulty is now to resolve whether he shall remove his family into ye country whither he is resolved to go and pass some days himself. In yt time I hope he may have my Lt. Portland's advice and yrs. which when you have thought all over as I have done I wish you may not find so much on both sides as to make it as difficult to resolve. It wld. be a great deal to be out of this melancholy scene in good air and to have the children out of the Town yt begins to grow very sickly ye great want
is somebody in ye house to have some care of ye children and be sometimes with him. If I were younger and had better health I would offer myself and Bridget for the little time he will be there this summer, however I will go to Moore Park at ye same time and be with them as often as I can. I had great hopes of Mrs Garraway but yt cannot be and Mrs Ann Berkley is in the country, can you think of anybody else. I believe you will not dislike what your sister has done with Lay Harriet who my Lt. Berkeley expressed a great deal of concern to leave and would not have done upon any other sense but the thoughts of her going to the Waters, will I believe hinder ire sister's thoughts of the country this summer unless you should advise it; it is what we all want ire advice and I hope I shall have it in my power to be of any service till you come over. Mrs How is come and I have ye and 19 bottles of Spew watter a great many thanks and one word I beg of your own health to make use yourself of what you can say so much of to others and to remember as we pray every day yt God's will may be done the reasonable answer is to submit to it I never writ with worse pen and paper nor had less time to amend it. Adieu.
For the Countess of Portland at the Hague. Moore Park, August ye 3rd.

I could not be so good as my word on Friday have been hurried hither by my nephew's journey into Yorkshire sooner than I cared to come or to leave my friends att London. I hope nothing will change the resolution I left my Lord Berkeley in of coming to Henley Park next Friday and bringing my niece Harriet with him or I shd. have had no comfort in the thoughts of him coming down I fancy will be the last time he will see Henley Park which. he seems to think so desolate a place to live in with so lonely a family in which. I cannot but agree with him though I do not know what change it would make if it were possible for him to keep the company he brings down with him which he seems to like better than every other. My niece before that was proposed had thoughts of taking Miss Anne and her nurse while my Lt. was in the Country which would have been very well liked but don't mention anything write but to myself where your letter will be safe. You need have no reserve, I found my Lord Berkeley had a good company last time I was there considering the emptiness of the Town and Mrs Garaway is seldom from him all I could perceive him at all revived was with Mr. Berkeley's coming; who you know is the best child in the world and I was very sorry that he and Mr. William were to leave him so soon. I found Moore Park what I am always pleased to see and the care they have to keep it in order looks as if they grew kind to it, I find ye boy what I like very well, so of ye other I can say nothing but yt she grows without improving any other way wh. will make it every day more melancholy. I have now a letter from Lt. Berkeley that tells me La. Harriet
is now with La. Biron wh. is the best place she can be in att London. I hope that nothing will alter my niece Lucy's coming with my Lt. Berkeley. I don't doubt but there are duch letters before this, but I have 3 days to expect whatever comes with them yt everybody is now so impatient off, pray God send me yt of ire being well I am so much more myself of late it makes me in pain for you yt must often now afford me two or three lines since I am less in the way of hearing of you from anybody else. My nephew and niece have been with Mrs How at ye Holt who I fancy I shall se soon they say Mrs How has grown very fat I wish you may not think more of your friends so when we meet, I hope ye news is true from ye Hague the Yacht is to go for you the middle of this month you were never so much wished for nor wanted by yrs.

note.value: LADY GIFFARD'S LETTER TO MRS. TEMPLE.

text.p: July ye 23 1715 .

I am very glad More Park has been revived with so good company but one must expect no satisfaction in this world without some alloy yours I doubt has had a sensible one with ire news of ire sister's being come to Town with so ill health which I shall think without a miracle, in a close lodging & this season one could not hope ire Doctor's skill great enough to relieve her, I cannot tell you I have seen her & am in doubt whether you may not have bin tempted to make another journey though you found so little reason to like ire last which am ashamed of myself at this distance she thought of so ineasy & have
had other hindrances this week, but have sent today to know when she goes out of Town since she would not accept my invitation to change ye scene a little and of passing some time here with me wh. is her natural air, before she returned to a place in wh. she has thought herself dyeing almost ever since she came into it. You hear how Dr. Mead has declared against Dr. Ratliff's advice of her going to ye Bath so yt I don't know from what we are left in hope of any relief which I find you agree with me in having expected from that.

I think all diseases look desperate at this time and wish there may not be one in ire sister as hopeless as any other wish yt may be passing too much of my time, only with ye entertainment of my own thoughts, but fear tic, and conclude as I think very reasonably from all ye disorders one hears of that I shall never bee quiet again, and if I may be allowed to say what so many conclude tic ye pursuit of so many to ye scaffold yt has brought it upon us.

The Duke of Ormond has at last thought fit to disappear, which his friends wish had bin sooner. He went from ye Lodge where he had bin all ye summer last Wednesday alone in a hackney coach not followed by any of his servants nor knew that he was gone till two days after the writs against him were to be sent up next day but the House will now find other employment of wh. ye papers and His Majesties speech will give you an account and we here of ye Pretender in one day in England and another in Scotland and talked of they say as familiarly at London as King William was before he came.

This subject is not very entertaining we shall leave it to tell you Mrs. More has prevailed with her husband to let her pass so many days here once in three years she could tell me no news from Moreparke which would have made her more welcome. I wish I had better to send you yt I hope to hear from tomorrow. I made my niece Temple your reproaches who said yt she had writ yt day and is always full of company. I have not yt complaint
nor thank God any other yt is not much less then I have reason to expect, but being at so much greater distance than usual from all my friends and particularly those at More Park to whom I am ever a most affectionate faithful servant. For Mrs. Temple, at More Park, near Farnham, Surrey.

The only reason that kept me from writing to you Dear Madam was the fear I had of troubling you, but I cannot forbear any longer from telling you how sure a sense I have of your misfortune I shall always be most heartily sorry for any thing that afflicts you but in this I think myself particularly concerned for both my Lord and I have lost a friend wee had a very real esteem and kindness for and shall ever have so for his memory I will say no more on so sad a subject but end this with begging you to believe that no body living is more sincerely your faithful Humble servant,
E. Somerset.
Feb. 4th. My Lord presents his humble service to your Lap and bids me tell you he shall think it a good fortune if he be capable in any kind to serve you.
For my Lady Giffard at Moore Park near Farnham in Surrey.

note.value: LETTER FROM THE DUCHESS OF SOMERSET.

text.p: London, June 7th - 26th.

You are very much in the right Dear Madam in believing you have bin in my thoughts for as soon as I saw the tittle of the book you mention in the advertisement I was afraid it was something put out without your approbation, and that you would be uneasy to se in print. I have not yet had time to read any of it but I am sorry to find by your letter that it is the dame you were
so obliging as to entrust with the Duke of Somerset though you were unwilling anybody else should see it. I remember we both agreed with you that it was not proper to be made public during my Aunt Essex's life and I am sure Doctor Swift has too much wit to think it is, which makes his having don it unpardonable and will confirm me in the opinion I had before of him that he is a man of no principle either of honour or religion but my Aunt or my Lord Essex I dare say will not think you had any part in it, for those that know you can never believe you guilty of breach of friendship for though some have grown cold to you I am sure the failing has bin on on their side not yours.

I have not yet heard anybody speak of this book but if I doe you may be sure I will doe you justice. If the Queen holds her resolution of going to Windsor a Thursday I shall go to Zion that day and shall be very glad to se you there a Friday or any other day except Saturday. - I am dear Madam, most faithfully, Ire. servant.
To My Lady Giffard at East Sheen.
For the Lady Giffard, at her house at Sheen. Petworth, August 18th.

I have so sensible a feeling of everything that tutsches you that I am truly sorry for the loss you have of my Lady Dixwell and that there has bin an aggravation of the unfortunate accident which you say was the occasion of her death, for though it is very terrible to lose a friend any way yet when it is by a natural disease one is better able to soport it because it is what we know must happen to us all if wee are not carried of some other way. I did not hear Lady Carlisle had any thoughts of leaving Kensington till she went to settle in London it is so pretty a place I wonder she should leave it for Richmond I believe you will see her often when she is there. I find it so much the fashion to go to France this summur but I thought your neighbours had bin too old to make journeys of pleasure into another Kingdom, and I think they choose a very ill time now there is so raging a distemper in some parts between Callis and Paris that few people are willing to travel that way. I hope the sea will keep us from any infection from thence. I have not seen the Dutchese of Richmond this month, but when I did she was in the best humour I ever saw and I hear from some of my neighbours that have seen her lately that she seems so well pleased with the report of her sons being to marry my Lord Cadogen's daughter that I dare say it is true. I find you have not bin less uneasy with the hot weather than my self, I have felt nothing like it this twenty year and what was the most surprising was that the nights were as hot as the days and the storms of thunder and lightning very
terrible and the sad effects one hears of it from several places will make me more afraid of it than ever. I thank God there has bin no hurt dun near us. I did not hear anything of the Duchess of Montague, but from you, if she was struck down it is being happy ever to recover for few people doe when lightning has so great an effect as to make them swooned except it proceeded from being mightily frighted. There was a buck killed which you were to have had part of but it not proving so good as some we have had the Duke of Somerset would not let it bee sent but you shall be sure to have some in a few days from - Dear Madam, Ire most affectionate humble servant,
E. Somerset.
To Lady Giffard att Shene. Petworth, July 23rd.

I have often heard you say that writing is an entertainment to you and now you have so few neighbours of your side of the watter you have more time then you use to have and if dear Lady Giffard could be sensible how welcome your letters are to me you would let me hear much oftener from you for I am too old to follow the raining custom of the age we live in of leaving friends I have had long acquaintance with for new ones and you shall always find me the same to you I have bin for so many years.

I have not heard from Lady Carlisle since I wrote to her, but I am glad to know from you that she is well and likes her habitation at Twickenham. I doe entirely agree with you that being quite alone is too melancholy a way of living but of the two I think that is more tolerable then so much company as there is now about here and particularly when it is dangerous to be abroad in an evening, which is not to be avoided now that everybody keep so late hours in the country as well as in London. When
I came hither there was such an appearance of fruit on all the trees that I was afraid when it was ripe I should have bin tempted to have eat too much of it but the continual rain and high winds has made such a destruction that I don't believe we shall have any good this year for that little which is now ripe has no taste and the rest is so spoiled that if we should have warm weather I don't think it could recover the blites there has bin. I never felt such a summur as this month that use to be the hottest has bin so cold that I could some days have sat by a fire, and have seldom had a window open though you know my rooms lye to the south and are warm when any place is so. Venison is the only thing that has not suffered by this unnatural weather and I hope you will find this good which I now send you. There is two pigs kept at Zion for you and whenever there is anything you would have that I can supply you with pray let me know it.

The Duke of Portland having deferred his journey so long I did not believe he intended to go and I am sorry to find he dus, for I can't see any prospect of advantage he can expect from it. I think it is against the opinion of all his friends and his being so set upon having this government looks as if there were an unlucky fate attended him to doe every thing to complete his undoing which I really believe this will for if there were much to be got there he is not of a temper to take the right way for he is the vainest man living and will spend whatever he gets and since he could not keep out of debt with so plentiful a fortune as his Father left him it is not very likely he will bee so good a manager as to repair it by his own industry, the near relation I have to him and his wife makes me heartily sorry for them I believe his being ill gave a great alarm to the Princess for he dus not appear to be a strong man and I think was often out of order last winter and the walking so late in the wood as they doe in such a cold weather season as this has bin must
certainly be very unwholesome though nobody likes better to be abroad in a fine evening than I doe. There has bin so few this summur that I have walked seldomer than ever I did, though I have bin well and not had a cold since I came into the country.
The Duke of Somerset sends his humble service to you, and I am, dear Madam, ire most faithful and affectionate servant,
E. S.
Petworth, Sept. 7th, 20.

You have reason to believe I have not bin well because tic so long since you heard from me, but I must own that was not the reason, nor I cannot give any good, therefore must depend entirely on Dear Lady Giffard's inclination to forgive the failings of your friends for I can say nothing for myself, as I have had no pain in my face since I came heather and have bin very well in my health. I have made use of the fine weather and walked more than I have don all the rest of the summer after so much cold as we had in July and August tic surprising at the end of September to feel the sun so hot as not to be able to walk but in the shade, it has had the same effect hear as in your garden for the grapes
begin to be ripe which I had despaired of this year, and wee have still the finest figs I ever eat!

I don't wonder Lady Carlisle is gon to London for if she is still lame that take away a great deal of the pleasure of being in the country, for I think being confined to sit in a chair makes company very necessary, and I believe there will soon be very little left either in Twitenham or Richmond, when the Court removes from thence you will lose the opportunity of seeing Lady Portland at Sheen, therefore as soon as ill weather comes you must think of taking up your winter's habitation in Dover Street, for the meeting of Parliament will bring everyone early to Town. Lady Carmarthen will be there next week and my daughter Wyndham the week after, but I have set no time for my leaving this place, but it will be not before the Duke of Somerset returns from Newmarket where he is going in ten days, he presents his humble service to you. I was surprised to hear Mr. Norton had prepared so fine an entertainment for the King, for he might safely imagine that a journey made in so much haste would not admit of staying to dine and a place where he did not intend to have lighted out of his coach, but I am glad he did for I think it so pretty a place as to be very well worth seeing; and the Prince was certainly very much in the right in what he said of Mr. Norton, for I don't know anybody who knows better how to behave themselves on all occasions then he does which makes some actions of his life the more unpardonable. I am sorry to hear Mrs. Talbot is so ill. I wish the Bath waters may doe her good I think she has bin there once before and was better after it, the troble she has lately had for the loss of two such friends I believe has had a great effect on her health. I hope my having bin so long without answering your first letter will not make you be so to me for I assure you Dear Madam the hearing from you is at all times a pleasure too - Your most affectionate humble servant,
E. Somerset.

note.value: LAST LETTER FROM THE DUCHESS OF SOMERSET

text.p: Petworth, June 20th 1722 .

I think myself very unlucky, dear madam, not to have seen you the day you were in Town, nor at Sheen, for if I had gon out of London the day I intended, I should have bin one day at Zion, and then my design was to have dined with you, and to have desired my Lady Carlisle to have meet me, and in the afternoon to have made poor Lady Scarborough a visit, when I believe you would both have liked to have gon with me, but I was disappointed of all this by hearing Lady Thomond would be in Town a Thursday, which made me put of my journey to see her, and a Friday I had only time to stop at Zion for two hours, and went on to Guilford that night, and the next day I dined here, and found the sweet air of the country very refreshing, and bin very well since I came here. I can't say I have bin for many months free from a pain in my face, but it is now so much less than it has bin, that if it does not grow worse, I shall think I have reason to be contented.

I am very glad to hear Lady Carlisle is better, for she has looked so ill this winter, that I thought her in great danger of a consumption, and she has so many valuable qualities that tic impossible to know her without having a true concern for her. I believe Lady Portland is very
happy when she can have liberty to pass a few hours with you. I pity her that she is obliged to go so often betwixt Richmond and Kensington in the heate of the day, and through such a cloud of dust as there is on that road, if the accounts I heard of what the Duke of Marlborough has left be true, tic so vast a wealth as I believe no subject in England ever was possessed of. I don't wonder she is in great affliction for him, for she married him for love, and he has always made her so good a return as to deserve a continuance of her kindness, and though his ill health had very much affected his understanding, yet he had still enough to make him sensible of the care she had of him, and there is nothing tutchese so near as the parting with an old friend. I left Lady Carmarthen well, and very big, I hope with child, but she is not yet quick. One cannot be sure of it. It is what I shall be very glad of, because it will be a great pleasure to her and it is so to me to se an increase to my family. - I am, dear Lady Giffard's most affectionate, humble Servant,
E. Somerset.
